data.name: PANSTARRS: Nucleus
text:
Nucleus of PANSTARRS
Approximate size: 3 km
Cometary nuclei are 'dirty snowballs' - irregular chunks of ice, rock, and dust.
As they approach the Sun, surface ice sublimates, releasing gas and dust.
Note: The nucleus is far too small to show at scale with the coma.

data.name: PANSTARRS: Dust Tail
text:
Dust Tail (Type II) of PANSTARRS
Maximum length: ~9.3 million km
The dust tail is composed of small dust particles pushed by solar radiation pressure.
It curves slightly along the comet's orbital path and appears yellowish from reflected sunlight.
Dust particles are larger and slower than ions, creating the characteristic curved shape.

data.name: PANSTARRS: Ion Tail
text:
Ion Tail (Type I, Plasma Tail) of PANSTARRS
Maximum length: ~23.1 million km
The ion tail is composed of ionized gas molecules (CO+, H2O+, etc.) swept away by the solar wind.
It points directly away from the Sun and appears bluish from fluorescence of ionized gases.
The ion tail is typically straighter and longer than the dust tail, reaching millions of km in length.

_encyclopedia.Sun:
Horizons: 10. The star at the center of our solar system. To display structure and atmosphere select "Solar Shells".

* Missions:
  * Pioneer 5 (NASA/DOD, 1960): Measured magnetic field phenomena, solar flare particles, and ionization.
  * Helios 1 & 2 (DFVLR/NASA, 1974 & 1976): Studied solar wind, magnetic and electric fields, cosmic rays, and dust.
  * ISEE-3 (NASA, 1978): Observed solar phenomena in conjunction with Earth-orbiting satellites, comets.
  * Ulysses (ESA/NASA, 1990-2009): Observed the Sun's polar regions and the solar wind at high solar latitudes.
  * WIND (NASA, 1994-Present): Still active, it provides continuous measurements of the solar wind.
  * SOHO (Solar and Heliospheric Observatory) (ESA/NASA, 1995-Present): A continuous view from its core to the solar wind.
  * ACE (Advanced Composition Explorer) (NASA, 1997-Present): Measures particles from the solar wind and galactic cosmic rays.
  * Hinode (JAXA/NASA/ESA/STFC, 2006-Present): Explores the Sun's magnetic fields.
  * STEREO (Solar TErrestrial RElations Observatory) (NASA, 2006-Present): Imaging the 3D structure of coronal mass ejections.
  * Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) (NASA, 2010-Present): High-resolution images of solar flares and eruptions.
  * IRIS (Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph) (NASA, 2013-Present): Sun's lower atmosphere (chromosphere and transition).
  * Parker Solar Probe (NASA, 2018-Present): Flew through the corona to study coronal heating and solar wind acceleration.
  * Solar Orbiter (ESA/NASA, 2020-Present): Provides unprecedented insight into how our local star "works" with 10 science instruments.
  * PUNCH (Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere) (NASA, Launched March 2025): Will study the Sun's outer atmosphere.
  * Solar Polar Orbit Observatory (Planned 2029): Will study views of its polar regions.
_encyclopedia.Earth:
Horizons: 399. Our home planet, the third from the Sun.
* Earth-centered: do not select Earth; visualize shells at 0.02 AU.
* Heliocentric: select Earth with or without shells.
* Missions: Galileo, Cassini-Huygens, Rosetta, New Horizons, JUNO, Parker Solar Probe, Deep Impact, NEAR Shoemaker, Solar Orbiter.
_encyclopedia.PANSTARRS:
Horizons: C/2025 R3. Comet C/2025 R3 (PanSTARRS) is a hyperbolic Oort Cloud comet
discovered September 8, 2025, by the Pan-STARRS survey telescope at Haleakala, Hawaii.

* Pristine visitor: It traveled ~170,000 years from the Oort Cloud to reach the inner
  Solar System. This is its first and final visit.
* The Interstellar Exit: During its approach, Jupiter provided a massive gravitational
  slingshot—the same mechanism NASA used to send Voyager into interstellar space.
  This "kick" added enough orbital energy to push its eccentricity above 1.0, meaning
  it now exceeds solar escape velocity and will never return.
* Perihelion: April 19, 2026 at 0.499 AU (74.6 million km from the Sun).
* Closest approach to Earth (Verified): April 26, 2026, at 09:22 UTC. Distance: 0.489146 AU
  (73,175,295 km). This is the exact moment of perigee as recorded by JPL Horizons.
* Appearance: Gas-rich and dust-poor. Features a massive 10+ degree ion tail with a
  dual-ray structure. Green C2 coma and blue ion tail confirmed (APOD April 14, 2026).
* Visibility: Reached naked-eye mag 5.1 on April 11. Peak brightness (~mag 3.5) enhanced
  by forward scattering near perihelion.
* Observation: Best viewed from the Northern Hemisphere through mid-April; now
  transitioning to the Southern Hemisphere as it recedes into deep space.
* Nucleus: Estimated at 3-5 km; no precise measurement published as of late April 2026.

Horizons: 299. Second planet from the Sun, known for its thick atmosphere.

* Missions: Venera (USSR); Mariner 2, 5, 10; Pioneer Venus Project, Vega (USSR), Magellan, Galileo, Cassini-Huygens,
